title: Peace with God, and Two Men
sum: Paul turns from the argument of the first four chapters to its results. People who are justified by faith have peace with God, a standing in grace, a hope of sharing God's glory, and a joy that even holds in trouble, because God's love has been poured into their hearts by the Holy Spirit. The proof of that love is plain: Christ died for people who were weak, ungodly, sinners and enemies (5:1-11).

Then Paul draws a wide picture. Sin and death entered the world through one man, Adam, and spread to all. But the gift in Christ is not just a cancelling of the damage. It is greater: grace overflows where sin multiplied. The comparison of Adam and Christ (5:12-21) is one of the most debated passages in the Bible, because the churches have read the words "because all sinned" in different ways. Below are the readings, a card for each church's teaching, and a note on the word "all" in 5:18.
readings: Read as the end of one argument and the start of another

Many commentators (Moo, Dunn, Fitzmyer) take 5:1-11 as the result of 1:18-4:25 and the doorway to the new life of chapters 5-8. The words "Having been justified ... we have" gather what went before; the refrain "through our Lord Jesus Christ" in 5:1, 11, 21 holds the chapter together.
Read as a doctrine of sin

From Augustine on, the Western churches read 5:12-21 as the main New Testament text on original sin: all humans are born into Adam's condition and share in the effects of his fall. The Eastern churches read the same lines as a teaching on inherited death and corruption, not guilt. The Reformation churches and the Catholic Church agree on the fact of inherited sin while differing on what it is.
Read as a story of two ages

Käsemann and others, in an apocalyptic reading, see Adam and Christ as heads of two ages, with sin and death on one side and grace and life on the other, with the law caught between. On this reading Paul is less interested in how sin passes on than in who rules: death, sin, or grace.

views.H: Paul writes from Corinth in the winter of about 56-57 to house churches in a capital whose emperor promised peace and called himself savior. "Peace," "boasting" and "ruling" are words with a public ring in Rome. Many of the readers were Jews who had come back after Claudius's expulsion (Acts 18:2), and they knew Adam from the Genesis story and from Jewish writings such as Wisdom of Solomon 2:24 ("death came into the world through the devil's envy") and Sirach 25:24. Two Jewish books written a generation or so after Paul, 4 Ezra 7:118 and 2 Baruch 54:15-19, show the same debate about Adam still going on. Gentile believers who had learned Genesis in the synagogues knew it too.
views.C: The text is secure apart from small points: 5:1 "we have" or "let us have" peace, and whether "by faith" belongs to 5:2 (see the variants). The sentence of 5:12 breaks off after the first half of its comparison; 5:13-17 are an interruption, and the "so also" returns in 5:18. A few scholars have suggested that 5:12-14 is an insertion, but no manuscript supports that.
views.L: Paul uses a rabbinic style of argument called "light to heavy" (qal vahomer): if the lesser is true, the greater is more so. The "how much more" in 5:9, 10, 15, 17 is the engine. The Adam-Christ section is a comparison (a synkrisis) built on contrasts: one man / one man, trespass / act of righteousness, disobedience / obedience, condemnation / justification, death rules / grace rules.
views.J: Jewish readers know the idea that death came through Adam and also that each person is responsible (a Jewish book written about AD 100, a generation after Paul, says in 2 Baruch 54:19: "each of us has become our own Adam"). The rabbis taught an evil inclination (the yetzer hara) that is present from birth and can be resisted with the help of Torah, but they did not teach inherited guilt. Paul's claim that death ruled "from Adam until Moses" (5:14) puts the law in the middle of history, not at the start. Because Adam is the ancestor of all, his story speaks to Paul's Gentile readers as well as his Jewish ones.
views.T: Origen, in Rufinus' Latin, already tied the baptism of infants to the stain of Adam's sin. Ambrosiaster and Augustine read the Latin "in whom all sinned"; Pelagius read the verse of imitation; the Greek fathers such as Chrysostom spoke of inherited death. The Council of Carthage (418), the Second Council of Orange (529), the Council of Trent (session 5), the Augsburg Confession (II), the Westminster Confession (6) and Wesley's Doctrine of Original Sin (1757) are the main later statements. Barth read 5:12-21 through Christ, not Adam.

deep.b:
The passage is a chain of contrasts, and Paul says outright that Adam is "a figure of the one who was coming" (5:14). But the likeness is not exact: in each pair the second member is larger.

  • One man, one man: Adam (5:12, 14, 15, 17, 19) and Jesus Christ (5:15, 17, 19).
  • One trespass, one act of righteousness (5:18): the first brings condemnation, the second justification that gives life.
  • Disobedience, obedience (5:19): the many were made sinners, the many will be made righteous.
  • The rule of death, the rule of grace (5:14, 17, 21): the word "rule as king" is used for both.
  • Not like, much more (5:15-17): the gift is out of proportion to the trespass, and it covers "many trespasses" (5:16), not only the first.

The place of the law is a side note, but a big one: death ruled before the law (5:13-14); the law came in so that the trespass would multiply (5:20); and grace overflowed beyond that. Chapter 7 returns to the law and what it did.

deep.h: 'Because all sinned': from the Latin to the churches
deep.b:
The Greek eph' ho pantes hemarton (5:12) is the hinge of the long history of original sin. The Latin Bible had in quo omnes peccaverunt, "in whom all sinned." Ambrosiaster (about 380) took it so, and Augustine, who knew the Greek only slightly, built on it in his fight with Pelagius (On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, 411-412). Pelagius, who read Greek well, held that Adam gave a bad example and that people sin by imitating him. The Council of Carthage condemned Pelagianism in 418. The Second Council of Orange (529) taught that Adam's sin harmed all his descendants in body and soul.

In the East, the Greek fathers read the verse as saying that death passed to all because of Adam, and that each person then sins; the modern Orthodox name for this is "ancestral sin." At the Reformation, the Lutherans and the Reformed held to inherited guilt and corruption; Arminius and Wesley held to inherited corruption with grace restoring a measure of freedom to all, and the Anabaptists generally denied that infants are guilty. Most modern commentators read eph' ho as "because" and still disagree about how "all sinned" is true of infants and others. This site's notes on 5:12 and the card below give the churches' own words.

deep.title: Spec: whose throne is 'death rules' written against?
deep.b: Claude's theory, not an established reading. In eight verses (5:14-21) Paul uses the verb basileuo, "rule as king," five times, and puts death, sin, grace and believers in the throne. He writes to a city where the emperor was celebrated as "lord," "savior" and bringer of peace. I think a first hearer in Rome could not miss that Paul is giving the title of ruler to powers other than Caesar, and that he is saying who the real rulers of human life are. If so, 5:1-11 (peace) and 5:12-21 (rule) answer the empire's boast in two steps. This overlaps with work by N. T. Wright, Robert Jewett and Neil Elliott on Paul and the Roman empire; they would add that the point is a quiet one, not a slogan. The evidence for it is only in the words, since Paul does not name Caesar here.

echoes: Genesis 2:16-17; Genesis 3:1-24; Isaiah 53:11-12; 1 Corinthians 15:21-22; 1 Corinthians 15:45-49; Philippians 2:8; Galatians 3:19; Wisdom of Solomon 2:23-24; Sirach 25:24; 4 Ezra 7:116-118; 2 Baruch 54:15-19

settings.what: Peace, hope and boasting in God
settings.to: the believers in Rome, Jews and Gentiles together, as it was read aloud in their house churches
settings.when: after the argument of 1:18-4:25 that Jews and Gentiles are both under sin and both justified by faith
settings.why: to show what the justification argued in chapters 1-4 gives a person here and now: peace, a place to stand, hope, and a joy that survives trouble. For readers who were divided over Jewish and Gentile ways, it names a ground they shared: all had been enemies, and all were reconciled by one death.
settings.readers: The Romans were a small, mixed and often strained group in a great city, and some had been through the expulsion under Claudius. The "troubles" of 5:3 were their own: poverty, suspicion from neighbors and the synagogues, and the pressure of the empire's cults.
views: Most commentators (Moo, Dunn, Fitzmyer, Wright, Jewett) treat chapters 5-8 as one main division of the letter. They differ over whether 5:1-11 mainly sums up the argument of 1:18-4:25 or opens the new division. Both agree that 5:1 begins with 'therefore.'

settings.to: the believers in Rome, Jews and Gentiles, who knew Adam from the Genesis story and from Jewish writings (Gentile believers through the synagogue)
settings.when: as he moves from 'we are saved' to 'why the old world was bound to sin and death, and how the new one is given'
settings.why: to show that the gospel is not about two peoples only (Jews and Gentiles) but about humanity as a whole, whom one man's act ruined and another's act restored. On the usual reconstruction (Dunn and many others, from chapters 14-15), this helped the Roman house churches, divided over Torah and food, to see themselves as one new human family under Christ. It also prepares the questions of chapter 6 (shall we sin?) and chapter 7 (what is the law for?).
settings.readers: Jews and Gentiles in Rome would have heard "one man" as an answer to the claims of both the empire (one ruler) and the tribal divisions inside the church (Jew and Gentile).
views: Adam as a person or a figure

The passage is read with Adam as the first man (most of the church fathers and the older confessions) or as the figure of humanity (Barth, and many modern writers). Paul's argument holds in both readings; the site gives no verdict.
Were the Roman churches divided over Torah and food?
Most commentators think so, from chapters 14-15 and from the history of the expulsion under Claudius. Mark Nanos and others dispute this reconstruction. Nothing in 5:12-21 depends on it.

traditions.q: Do all people inherit Adam's sin and guilt (5:12)?
views: Original sin is "contracted" and not "committed": a state, not a personal act. Adam's sin was passed to all by descent, so that every person is born deprived of original holiness, wounded in nature and inclined to sin. Baptism removes original sin but a pull toward sin (concupiscence) remains, which is not itself sin (Catechism 402-406, 1264; Council of Trent, session 5; Second Council of Orange, 529).

The East speaks of "ancestral sin": what Adam passed on is mortality, corruption and a bent toward sin, not personal guilt. Each person is guilty of his own sins. Orthodox teachers (Romanides, Meyendorff, Ware) point out that the Latin "in whom all sinned" of 5:12 is not in the Greek.

All people born in the ordinary way are born with sin, "without fear of God, without trust in God, and with concupiscence," and this disease brings condemnation to those not born again by baptism and the Spirit (Augsburg Confession II). The Formula of Concord (Solid Declaration I) says original sin is a deep corruption of the whole person, not only an outward fault.

Adam was the covenant head of the human race, and his first sin was counted to all his descendants, who are conceived in sin and by nature children of wrath, with their nature corrupted (Westminster Confession 6.3-4; Heidelberg Catechism 7-8).

Original sin "standeth not in the following of Adam, (as the Pelagians do vainly talk;) but it is the fault and corruption of the Nature of every man, that naturally is engendered of the offspring of Adam." The infection remains even in the baptized (Thirty-Nine Articles, Article 9).

Wesley taught that human nature is truly corrupted by Adam, but that God's free gift in Christ, working as "prevenient grace," gives every person some measure of light and freedom, so that no one is condemned only for Adam's sin (Wesley, The Doctrine of Original Sin; Articles of Religion, article 7).

Baptist confessions agree on the fall but are slower to speak of inherited guilt. The Baptist Faith and Message (2000, article 3) says Adam's descendants inherit "a nature and an environment inclined toward sin" and "as soon as they are capable of moral action, they become transgressors and are under condemnation."

The Dordrecht Confession (1632) teaches that the fall brought sin and death on all of Adam's descendants and that grace in Christ is offered to all. Mennonite teaching has generally held that young children are covered by Christ's atonement until they can choose for themselves.
The Second Article of Faith says, "We believe that men will be punished for their own sins, and not for Adam's transgression." The fall is understood as a necessary step in God's plan.

traditions.q: Does Christ's one act of righteousness bring justification to all people (5:18)?
views: Christ died for all and God wants all to be saved, but not all will be: hell is a real possibility, and "God predestines no one to go to hell." The Church has never declared any individual damned and condemned the teaching of Origen that all would be restored in the end (Catechism 605, 1037, 1058; Council of Constantinople, 543).

The Fifth Council (553) is understood to have condemned the "restoration of all" taught by Origen. Yet Gregory of Nyssa is a saint, and some Orthodox writers (Bulgakov, and Kallistos Ware in "Dare We Hope for the Salvation of All?") allow a hope for all while denying that the Church teaches it.

Christ's death atoned for the sins of the whole world, and the gospel is offered to all; faith receives it (Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration XI). Some Lutheran bodies speak of an "objective justification" of the whole world, which faith receives.

Calvin wrote that Paul makes grace common to all because it is offered to all, not because it in fact reaches all. The Canons of Dort say Christ's death is of infinite worth and enough for the whole world, but effective for the elect only (Dort II.3, 8). Karl Barth taught that all are elected in Christ and refused to say that all will be saved.

Christ's atonement is for all and may be received by all through the grace given to all; Wesley preached "free grace" against predestination (Sermon 128, 1739). Not all will be saved, since grace can be resisted.

Baptists are divided. General Baptists hold that Christ died for all. Particular (Reformed) Baptists hold that he died effectively for the elect. The Baptist Faith and Message (2000, article 4) says "salvation is offered freely to all who accept Jesus Christ as Lord and Saviour."

title: Dead to Sin, Alive to God
sum: Chapter 5 ended with grace overflowing where sin multiplied. Paul expects the objection: then why not sin more, so that grace can overflow even more? "By no means!" His answer begins with baptism. Those who were baptized into Christ were baptized into his death; they were buried with him and raised with him to a new way of living. Sin is a master that no longer has a claim on them.

In the second half (6:15-23) Paul uses the slave market for his picture. Everyone is a slave to something. Before, it was sin, and its pay was death. Now believers have been handed over to righteousness, and the result is holiness and eternal life. The chapter ends on one of the best-known lines in the Bible: sin pays wages, but God gives a gift.
readings: Read as a baptism text
The churches read 6:3-11 as the main New Testament text on what baptism means: death and burial with Christ and a rising to new life. They disagree on how baptism does this (see the card).
Read as an answer to an objection

6:1 and 6:15 are the same question, "Shall we sin?" Paul answers twice with "By no means!" and a reason each time: you died to sin, and you cannot serve two masters. The chapter is less about the rite than about identity.
Read as the picture of a slave market
The second half works only if the reader knows how slavery worked in Rome: handing over, obeying, wages, freedom by purchase. Paul says he uses a human picture and apologizes for its weakness (6:19).

views.H: Roman house churches included slaves and freed slaves. A slave's status was settled by sale, owner's will or manumission; wages (opsonia) were a soldier's pay. Baptism in the first century was probably by immersion in running or still water (Didache 7 gives a later rule), and the rite was a public moment for the new believer.
views.C: 6:17 is a rare case where Paul speaks of a "form of teaching" that new believers received, which some think points to a baptismal catechism. Small variants appear at 6:11 and 6:12, where the Byzantine text adds "our Lord" and "it in" (see the variants). 6:13 and 6:19 both use the same unusual plural of the body's "parts" (melē).
views.L: The chapter has two panels, each opening with the same question (6:1, 6:15) and the same "By no means!" The argument runs in a ring: death to sin (6:2-11), a command (6:12-14), a slave image (6:15-23). 6:23 closes with the refrain "in Christ Jesus our Lord."
views.J: Jewish readers know a rule, recorded in the Talmud long after Paul (about AD 500-600), that death frees from the commandments (Shabbat 30a; Niddah 61b), and the idea of Torah as a yoke. "Walk" for the way of life is the Hebrew halak, the root of halakhah. Some Paul-within-Judaism writers (Nanos and Gager, for example) argue that "under law" in 6:14 refers to a Gentile's position, not a Jew's obligation. The text is not written to tell Jews to leave the Torah.
views.T: Lectures attributed to Cyril of Jerusalem explained the baptism ritual to new Christians by this chapter (Mystagogical Catecheses 2): going down into the water three times pictured the three days in the tomb. Tertullian (On Baptism) and Augustine used it against those who thought grace allowed sin. Luther's Small Catechism uses 6:4 for the daily death of the old Adam. Calvin used it for "mortification and vivification."

deep.h: Paul's three answers to 'Shall we sin so that grace may multiply?'
deep.b:
Paul does not argue from the law, which he has just said is not our rule (6:14). He gives three arguments.

  1. Who you are (6:2-11). You died with Christ, so you are no longer in the sphere where sin rules. Baptism is the moment this is made plain. The picture is not of becoming perfect but of changing masters.
  2. What you are to do (6:12-14). The command comes after the fact: "Do not let sin be your king." The believer is told to present the parts of the body, as weapons or tools, to a new commander.
  3. Whom you serve (6:15-23). Everyone obeys someone; the only question is whom. The wages of the old master are death; the gift of the new is eternal life.

Paul's reasoning shows that he held grace and obedience together. For him they are not opposites: "obedience of faith" (1:5) is the frame of the whole letter.

Paul does not describe the rite. Later writers do. The Didache (late first or early second century) says to baptize "in running water" if possible, or in other water, and to pour water three times if there is not enough. The lectures attributed to Cyril of Jerusalem (about 350) describe the person stripped, anointed, and plunged three times, and links the three plunges with Romans 6. Tertullian (about 200) argued for delaying baptism for children and the unmarried; Origen thought that infant baptism was an apostolic custom. The churches' differences today, on infants, on immersion, on what the rite does, all go back to different readings of this chapter. See the card and the baptism topic.

echoes: Genesis 3:1-24; Psalm 1; Isaiah 50:1; 1 Corinthians 10:1-2; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Galatians 2:19-20; Galatians 3:27; Colossians 2:12; Colossians 3:1-4; Ephesians 4:22-24; Mishnah Avot 3:5; Didache 7

settings.what: Dead to sin: the answer to 'Shall we sin so that grace may multiply?'
settings.to: the believers in Rome, with an imaginary objector in view (the 'diatribe'); the charge goes back to what critics said about Paul himself (3:8)
settings.when: right after 5:20-21, which says that grace overflows where sin multiplies
settings.why: to show that grace does not excuse sin because it ends the rule of sin: those who have been joined to Christ in baptism have died to the power that held them. For Roman believers, some of them Jews who thought the law was the only barrier to sin and some Gentiles who thought freedom meant license, the argument says that the barrier is a new life from Christ.
settings.readers: Many of the Romans had been baptized without ever meeting Paul. He reminds them what the rite meant, which also showed that he and they shared a common baptism and a common faith.
views: The objector is a stand-in in the style of the diatribe (Stowers), or stands for opponents who had actually made the charge (3:8).

settings.what: Slaves of sin, slaves of righteousness
settings.to: the believers in Rome, many of them slaves or former slaves, in the capital, where slaves and freed slaves were numerous
settings.when: as the second form of the same question, after the first answer (6:1-14)
settings.why: to make the point that no one is free of masters; the only choice is whom you serve. This gave readers who knew the slave market a picture of freedom as a change of owner, and it said that obedience to God is the way to the life that sin could not give. Paul says that he uses a human picture and apologizes for its weakness (6:19).
settings.readers: The slave's "wages" and the freed slave's duties were part of daily life in Rome. The word for "wages" was a soldier's pay, which Roman believers also knew.
views: Paul uses slavery as a picture without commenting on the institution. Later readers have debated whether this endorses it; see the notes at 6:16 and the topic on slavery.

traditions.q: What does baptism do, if believers are "buried with him" through it (6:3-4)?
views: Baptism is the sacrament in which a person dies and rises with Christ. It forgives original sin and all personal sin and gives new birth in the Spirit. The Catechism uses Romans 6 for the picture: immersion in water symbolizes burial into Christ's death, and rising from it a new creature (Catechism 1214, 1227, 1262-1263).

Baptism, by triple immersion, is a real sharing in Christ's death and resurrection. The newly baptized, including infants, are anointed with chrism and receive the Eucharist at once (Ware, The Orthodox Church).

Baptism "works forgiveness of sins, delivers from death and the devil, and gives eternal salvation to all who believe" (Small Catechism IV). Romans 6:4 is read as the meaning of the rite: the old Adam is drowned daily by contrition and repentance, and a new person rises. Infants are baptized.

Baptism is a sign and seal of the covenant of grace, a picture of union with Christ in death and new life; it does not itself regenerate. Infants of believers are baptized (Westminster Confession 28.1; Calvin, Institutes 4.15.5).
Baptism is "a sign of Regeneration or new Birth" by which those who receive it rightly are grafted into the Church. The baptism of young children is retained (Thirty-Nine Articles, Article 27).
The Articles of Religion (1784, Article 17) call baptism not only a sign of profession but "a sign of regeneration or the new birth," and say that the baptism of young children is to be retained.

Baptism is the immersion of a believer, a picture of the burial and resurrection of Christ and of the believer's own death to sin; it is an ordinance, not a means of saving grace (Baptist Faith and Message, 2000, article 7).

Baptism is given to those who have been taught repentance and change of life, who believe that their sins are taken away by Christ, and who wish to "walk in the resurrection of Jesus Christ" (Schleitheim Confession, 1527, article 1). Infant baptism is rejected.

Water baptism by immersion is an ordinance for believers, a witness to the death and resurrection of Christ. Pentecostals distinguish it from baptism in the Holy Spirit (Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths).

title: The Law and the Divided 'I'
sum: Paul has said that believers have died to sin (chapter 6) and are "not under law" (6:14). Is the law then the enemy? Chapter 7 answers: no, the law is holy, righteous and good. He starts with an example from marriage: death ends a legal bond (7:1-6). Then he tells a story in the first person: the commandment came, sin used it, and "I died" (7:7-13). Finally the story turns to the present tense and the "I" cries out in a divided will: "What I want to do, I do not do. What I hate, that is what I do" (7:15).

No passage in Romans has divided readers more. Who is the "I"? Adam, Israel, Paul as a Christian, Paul before Christ, a figure of speech? The answer is not settled by grammar. This page gives the readings, with the churches' answers on the card and a deep dive below.
readings: Read as the struggle of a Christian

Augustine in his later work, Luther, Calvin and many Protestant commentators (Murray, Cranfield) hear a believer who delights in God's law and still finds the flesh fighting back. The present tense, the "delight" of 7:22 and the "thanks" of 7:25 are their main evidence.
Read as life under the law before Christ

Origen, Chrysostom, Wesley and many modern scholars (Kümmel, Käsemann, Moo and many Catholic commentators) read it as the picture of a person under the law, seen from the standpoint of Christ. The "sold under sin" of 7:14 and the "no good lives in me" of 7:18 seem too strong for a believer.
Read as a figure: Adam, Israel, or a speaking part

A third group sees the "I" as Adam (the echoes of Genesis 2-3 in Romans 7:9-11), Israel at Sinai (N. T. Wright), or a speech-in-character (Stanley Stowers: a Gentile who tries to keep the law). On these readings the "I" is not autobiography.

views.H: In a city of Jews and Gentiles, "law" meant more than one thing: the Torah for Jewish believers, the Torah as learned by Gentile "God-fearers," Roman law for everyone. The marriage example (7:1-3) fits both Roman and Jewish rules of marriage; Jewish divorce and widowhood law is in the Mishnah (Kiddushin 1:1; written down about AD 200, but recording older law). Greek and Roman writers also described the divided will (Euripides, Ovid, Epictetus).
views.C: Almost every scholar since Kümmel (1929) agrees that the "I" of 7:7-25 is not simple autobiography. Bultmann (1947) argued that 7:25b is a later gloss. There are variants at 7:6 ("we died" or "it died"), 7:14 ("made of flesh" or "fleshly"), 7:18 (a verb at the end) and 7:25 ("thanks" or "I thank"). The thanksgiving in 7:25a comes before the sentence that seems to restate the problem (7:25b).
views.L: The chapter is a short drama in three scenes: an illustration (7:1-6), a story of the commandment (7:7-13) with a defense of the law at each end (7:7, 7:12-13), and a monologue (7:14-25) ending in a cry and an answer. The cry "Who will rescue me?" is answered by 7:25a, and again by 8:1-2.
views.J: A Jewish reader hears Paul defend the Torah strongly (7:12, 14, 16, 22), and hears Paul's account of the evil inclination without the name: the rabbis taught a good and an evil inclination (yetzer) in every person, and Torah as the antidote (Kiddushin 30b, a Talmud passage written down centuries after Paul). Krister Stendahl argued that Paul, as a Jew, did not feel guilty about his own keeping of the law (Philippians 3:6), so 7:14-25 is not his autobiography.
views.T: Augustine's change of mind is the key piece of history. In his early work he read 7:14-25 of the unredeemed person; against Pelagius he read it of the believer. Aquinas knows both. Luther's phrase for the believer, "at once righteous and a sinner," rests on his reading of this passage. Calvin and the Reformed followed; Wesley and the holiness tradition read it as the person under the law, and chapter 8 as the life of one born of the Spirit.

deep.h: Who is the 'I' of Romans 7? Seven readings
deep.b:
1. Paul the believer. Augustine (after 396), Luther, Calvin, the Reformed confessions, John Murray, C. E. B. Cranfield, and in a form of his own, James Dunn (the "I" of a person living in two ages at once).
  2. Paul or any person before faith, seen from after. Origen, Chrysostom, Wesley, Kümmel, Käsemann, Douglas Moo, Joseph Fitzmyer. Paul looks back on life under the law in the light of Christ.
  3. Adam. The echoes of Genesis 2-3 in Romans 7:9-11 ("alive without law," the commandment, "tricked me," "I died") point to the first human. N. T. Wright and others give this a part.
  4. Israel at Sinai. The "I" is Israel, given the law and finding sin revived (Wright, The Climax of the Covenant).
  5. A rhetorical "I." Speech in character (prosopopoeia), a figure any reader can enter. Kümmel (1929) said it was every person without Christ; Stowers (1994) said it is a Gentile who tries to keep the law and fails.
  6. Paul as a child. The "I" is Paul before he reached the age of responsibility. This has little support among scholars.
  7. Paul, a Jew who did not feel guilty. Stendahl (1963) argued that the Western church read its own "introspective conscience" into Paul, who elsewhere says he was blameless under the law (Philippians 3:6). Many accept the point and still read the chapter as about someone else.

Many scholars hold that more than one is true: the "I" is an Adam-like figure whom Paul and his readers recognize in themselves. The Plain does not decide.

The word nomos occurs 28 times in chapters 7-8 (23 in chapter 7, 5 in chapter 8). It is "the law of Moses" for the most part, and the Plain keeps "law" throughout. But Paul uses it in odd phrases: "the law of my mind" (7:23), "the law of sin" (7:23, 25; 8:2), "the law of the Spirit of life" (8:2), and "this law" in 7:21. Some translators write "principle" for these (the way we say "the law of gravity"). Others see Paul playing on the word, using the Torah in different ways. Wright and Dunn argue that all uses still point to the Torah, now seen through the Spirit. The Plain's "law" lets the reader see the repeated word.

deep.title: Spec: the 'I' as a voice the Romans could each take up
deep.b: Claude's theory, offered as a synthesis and not a new reading. The Roman churches were mixed: Jews who had lived under the Torah, Gentile God-fearers who had learned it, and Gentiles who had not. Paul's 'I' is never named, and 7:1 says he speaks "to people who know law." I suggest that the 'I' is deliberately open, a voice in which Jewish readers could hear Adam and Sinai (7:9-13), and Gentile readers could hear their own failure to keep any moral law, with the same cry at the end for all. The strongest support is the change of tense and the lack of a name, and that the answer in 7:25 and 8:1-2 is the same for all. This overlaps with the speech-in-character reading of Stowers and the Adam-Israel reading of Wright. It cannot be proved from the text and would fail if the 'I' is plain autobiography.

echoes: Genesis 2:17; Genesis 3:13; Exodus 20:17; Deuteronomy 5:21; Deuteronomy 30:15-20; Jeremiah 31:31-34; Ezekiel 36:26-27; Psalm 1:2; Psalm 119; 2 Corinthians 3:6; Galatians 3:19-25; Philippians 3:6; Mishnah Kiddushin 1:1; Mishnah Avot 5:21

settings.what: The marriage illustration: released from the law
settings.to: 'those who know law': the Jewish believers and the Gentiles who had learned the Torah in the synagogues, in the Roman house churches
settings.when: after 6:14 ('You are not under law') raised the question of what the law now is
settings.why: to explain how believers can be 'not under law' without the law being an evil: a death ends a legal claim, as a husband's death frees his wife. The rule at stake is Torah marriage law (a wife is bound until her husband dies or divorces her; Mishnah Kiddushin 1:1) and similar Roman rules; it bound Jewish couples under Torah, and the Romans it was written to knew it from the synagogue or from their own law. The illustration frees the reader to belong to Christ and to bear fruit for God.
settings.readers: The mixed church had to ask how Jewish believers stood toward the Torah now. The marriage image says that the relationship has changed and not that the law is bad.
views: Many readers take 'law' as the Torah that bound Israel and reads it for Jewish believers; 'Paul within Judaism' writers (Nanos, Gager) take Paul to be speaking mainly to Gentile believers about law as a power over those outside Israel's covenant. The question is argued in Dunn and Fredriksen.

settings.to: the same readers, as a story anyone can follow
settings.when: as the answer to 'Is the law sin?' (7:7)
settings.why: to defend the law and say where the trouble lies: the law is holy, sin takes the commandment as a base of operations, and the result is death. For readers who knew the law as the way of life (Deuteronomy 30:15-20), this said that the law was good but could not make people good.
settings.readers: In a church with both Jewish and Gentile members the story spoke to each: Jews heard Adam and Sinai, Gentiles heard what any prohibition does.
views: Adam; Israel at Sinai; Paul as a child; every person; a rhetorical figure. See the deep dive.

settings.what: The divided 'I' and the cry for rescue
settings.by: Paul, in the first person present tense
settings.when: after the story of 7:7-13, as it turns to the present
settings.why: to show that the law cannot rescue anyone from the power of sin; only Christ can. The cry in 7:24 and the thanksgiving in 7:25 lead directly to 8:1 ('no condemnation') and to the life of the Spirit. For Roman readers it shows that Paul does not mean that they can be saved by keeping the law, Jewish or Roman, nor that the law is to blame.
settings.readers: The Romans, Jewish and Gentile, knew the experience of the divided will, which Greek and Roman writers also described. Paul gives it a name and an answer.
views: Believer or not yet a believer
The churches and the scholars divide. See the card below and the deep dive.

traditions.q: Who is the "I" of 7:14-25: a believer, or a person under the law before faith?
views: Both readings are found. Augustine's later view (the believer) is set beside the older view (the person under the law before grace) by Aquinas, and the Council of Trent teaches that the desire left in the baptized is not itself sin (session 5, §5). Fitzmyer and other modern Catholic commentators read the passage as the person under the law, before faith.

Chrysostom, and Origen before him (whose wider teaching the East later condemned), read the "I" as the person under the law before grace, and the Greek fathers generally follow this line. They do not deny that the Christian struggles with the passions.

Luther came to read the passage as the Christian, who is at once righteous and a sinner (simul iustus et peccator): the "spiritual man" is the one who finds the flesh still fighting. He changed his early view and did so on this text.

Calvin read 7:14-25 as the regenerate person, in whom the flesh still wars with the Spirit. The Westminster Confession says that in the regenerate "there abideth still some remnants of corruption" and a continual war between flesh and Spirit (13.2).

Article 9 says that "this infection of nature doth remain, yea in them that are regenerated" and that "concupiscence and lust hath of itself the nature of sin," language that fits the Augustinian reading. The Church of England does not require one reading of the passage.

Wesley taught that 7:14-25 describes a person under conviction of sin and under the law, not yet set free by faith; chapter 8 describes one born of the Spirit (Sermon 9, "The Spirit of Bondage and of Adoption"; Notes on the New Testament).
Baptist confessions (the Baptist Faith and Message, 2000; the Second London Confession, 1689) have no article on who the "I" of 7:14-25 is, and Baptist commentators read it both ways.
Evangelical scholars are divided: John Murray read the passage of the believer; Douglas Moo reads Paul as looking back on life under the law from the standpoint of Christ.

title: Life in the Spirit: No Condemnation
sum: After the cry of 7:24, chapter 8 answers: there is no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus. The law could not break the grip of sin, because the flesh made it weak. God did what the law could not, sending his Son, and now the Spirit lives in believers, gives them life, makes them God's adopted children and lets them cry "Abba, Father!" (8:1-17).

The second half widens. Present sufferings are weighed against coming glory, and the whole creation groans in labor with believers, waiting for freedom. The Spirit pleads when we cannot pray. God works all things together for good, for those he foreknew, decided beforehand, called, justified and glorified. The chapter ends with questions no one can answer: who can accuse, who can condemn, who can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord? (8:18-39).
readings: Read as the answer to chapter 7

Chapter 8 begins with "no condemnation" (8:1) and ends with "no separation" (8:35-39). On this reading it answers the cry of 7:24: the Spirit of life breaks the power of sin and death that the law could only expose.
Read as a theology of the Spirit

The Spirit appears nearly twenty times in 8:1-27, more than in any chapter of Paul's letters: the Spirit gives life, leads, witnesses, helps and pleads. For the Eastern church and the Pentecostal churches this is the center of the letter.
Read as a letter to a church under pressure

Many commentators note the vocabulary of suffering, hope, waiting and endurance: the Roman believers were a minority in a hostile city. The promises of 8:28-39 are given to people who suffer, not to the comfortable.

views.H: The chapter draws on Roman adoption and inheritance (8:15-17), on the language of the empire's triumph (8:37 "overwhelming victory"), and on the experience of believers who faced poverty, hostility and the sword (8:35). Nero's persecution of the Christians in Rome came only in AD 64 (Tacitus, Annals 15.44), several years after the letter. "Height" and "depth" in 8:38-39 may be astrological terms from a world that believed in fate (see the note at 8:38).
views.C: There are important textual variants: 8:1 (a clause the KJV adds), 8:2 ("you" or "me"), 8:11 ("because of" or "through" the Spirit), 8:23 ("adoption" missing in P46), 8:28 ("God works" or "all things work"), 8:34 ("Christ" or "Christ Jesus"). The punctuation of 8:33-34 (statement or question) is a separate choice for editors.
views.L: The chapter has a ring: "no condemnation" at the start (8:1), "who is there to condemn?" near the end (8:34). It has a chain of verbs (foreknew, decided beforehand, called, justified, glorified: 8:29-30) and a run of questions (8:31-35). It is also built from a series of groanings: creation (8:22), believers (8:23), the Spirit (8:26).
views.J: A Jewish reader hears Ezekiel's new spirit (Ezekiel 36:26-27; 37:14), Jeremiah's law on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33) and Isaac's binding behind 8:32. Psalm 44:22 in 8:36 was read by the rabbis of the martyrs. Jewish readers of the Spirit, adoption and creation will recognize themes of Israel as God's son and creation's renewal. For Paul within Judaism readers, the "children of God" of 8:14-17 are Gentiles, adopted into an existing family.
views.T: Chapter 8 is where the Eastern and Western churches draw different lines: for the East, theosis (8:17, 29-30); for the West, predestination, perseverance and assurance. Augustine, Aquinas, Luther ("the chief part of the New Testament" is Romans, and chapter 8 its core), Calvin, Wesley and Barth all lean on this chapter. Origen took the groaning creation as a sign of rational beings. Catholic teaching quotes it in the Catechism on the Spirit's prayer (741) and on divine adoption (1996).

deep.h: The groaning creation and the new creation
deep.b: Romans 8:19-22 is the Bible's clearest statement that the human story is tied to the rest of creation. Genesis 3:17-19 says the ground is cursed because of Adam; Isaiah 11:6-9 and 65:17-25 promise a world at peace; Revelation 21:1-5 shows the new heaven and earth. Paul's "futility" (mataiotes) is the Greek word for the Hebrew hevel of Ecclesiastes. His "bondage to decay" and "freedom" use the language of slavery and the exodus. His "labor pains" are the language of apocalyptic hope. The hope is not to escape the world but for the world itself to be set free. Christian writers have read the passage as a basis for care of creation (see the note at 8:22); Jewish readers will see the covenant with creation of Genesis 9 behind it.

deep.h: The 'golden chain' and what it does not say
deep.b: The five verbs of 8:29-30 are the most-quoted line on predestination in the Bible. Three things should be noticed. First, they are past tense for all five, though glorification is still future; Paul speaks as if the end is certain. Second, the aim of predestination is to be "formed to match the image of his Son" (8:29), a destination, not a list of names. Third, the verse says nothing about those who are not chosen; that is taken up in chapter 9. The traditions then read the chain differently: for the Reformed it is an unbroken line from a free choice to glory; for Arminians and Wesleyans, the chain concerns those who believe and persevere; for Catholics, predestination to glory is real but no one can claim to know his own; the Orthodox emphasize cooperation of grace and will. The card on this page gives each church's words.

Paul's word huiothesia comes from Roman law (see the note at 8:15 and the topic on adoption). He uses it in three places: the Spirit of adoption (8:15), the adoption still awaited (8:23), and the adoption that belongs to Israel (9:4). The idea is that God takes slaves and outsiders into his family and gives them the full rights of a son. Israel was called "my son" (Exodus 4:22); Paul says the Gentiles are now children in the same family. Adoption sits next to the "firstborn" of 8:29: Christ is the elder brother in a large family.

echoes: Genesis 1:26-27; Genesis 3:17-19; Genesis 22:12; Exodus 4:22; Isaiah 11:6-9; Isaiah 50:7-9; Isaiah 53:6; Isaiah 53:12; Isaiah 65:17-25; Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 36:26-27; Ezekiel 37:14; Psalm 44:22; Psalm 110:1; Psalm 118:6; Ecclesiastes 1:2; Mark 14:36; Galatians 4:4-7; Colossians 1:15; Revelation 21:1-5

settings.what: Life in the Spirit: no condemnation, adoption as children
settings.to: the believers in Rome, Jewish and Gentile together
settings.when: after the cry of 7:24 and its answer (7:25), as the climax of the first three movements of the letter
settings.why: to say what has been done in Christ (no condemnation, the law's requirement fulfilled, a new life) and to remind readers that they are God's adopted children, heirs with Christ, led by the Spirit. For Roman believers who felt like outsiders in a hostile city, and for Gentiles among Jews, it gave a place in the family.
settings.readers: The Romans knew adoption and inheritance as public legal acts. Slaves among them heard that the Spirit does not make them slaves again. Gentile believers heard that they inherit the promises given to Israel.
views: 8:15 'we cry' and Galatians 4:6 'he cries' are read as the Spirit speaking in believers, or as believers praying by the Spirit. See the note at 8:15.

settings.what: Suffering, the groaning creation, and God's purpose
settings.to: the believers in Rome, many of them poor and under pressure
settings.when: as Paul turns from the 'if we suffer with him' of 8:17 to the larger hope
settings.why: to say that present sufferings are not the last word, that creation and believers and the Spirit all groan toward the same freedom, and that God's purpose for his people will be completed. The words were meant to keep a small, uneasy group of believers going through trouble.
settings.readers: The Romans' "sufferings" were poverty, hostility and the risk of arrest. The Jewish believers among them also remembered the expulsion under Claudius (Acts 18:2).
views: The natural world (most), all humans, or the powers. See the note at 8:19.

settings.what: Who can separate us from the love of God?
settings.when: as the close of the argument of chapters 5-8 and the doorway into chapters 9-11
settings.why: to end the argument on the certainty of God's love: a series of questions that no hostile power can answer. For believers who faced the sword, hunger and fear, it said that these things cannot cut the tie. It also sets up chapters 9-11, where Paul asks the same about Israel.
settings.readers: The Romans lived in the empire's capital, where Caesar's power was everywhere. Paul lists the powers and says none of them can separate.
views: As an unconditional promise to the elect (Reformed); as a promise that no outside power can break the bond, though a person may turn away (Wesleyan, Catholic, Orthodox). See the card.

traditions.q: Can a believer be sure of being a child of God, as 8:15-16 suggests?
views: Grace belongs to the supernatural order and cannot be known with the certainty of faith unless God reveals it; we cannot rely on feelings or works to conclude that we are justified. The Church holds that a believer can have hope and a moral certainty without a guarantee (Council of Trent, session 6, chapter 9, canons 13-16; Catechism 2005).

Orthodox teaching speaks of hope and humility rather than a claimed certainty. Salvation is a lifelong process of becoming like God, and the saints feared to claim it. The Spirit's presence is known in the sacraments and in a life of prayer.

Faith is "a living, daring confidence in God's grace" (Luther's Preface to Romans). The Apology of the Augsburg Confession (IV) teaches that faith is trust that sins are forgiven for Christ's sake, so the believer rests on the promise rather than on inner feelings.

Assurance is possible and a duty: believers may be "certainly assured" that they are in a state of grace, and this is "an infallible assurance of faith" resting on the promises of God, the fruit of the Spirit and the Spirit's witness with their spirits (Westminster Confession 18.1-2).

Article 17 does not speak of assurance as such. It says that the thought of predestination is "full of sweet, pleasant, and unspeakable comfort" to "godly persons," and that for "curious and carnal persons" it can lead to despair or reckless living.
Wesley made "the witness of the Spirit" a main doctrine: an inward impression on the soul by which the Spirit witnesses to the believer's spirit that he is a child of God (Sermons 10-11).
Most Baptists teach assurance, resting on Scripture and the Spirit's witness; the Baptist Faith and Message (2000, article 5) says all real believers endure to the end.
The Spirit gives assurance of present salvation; many Pentecostal churches teach that it is conditional on continuing in faith (Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths).

traditions.q: How do foreknowledge, predestination and calling fit together (8:29-30)?
views: "Foreknew" means God's loving choice beforehand. God chose his people before the foundation of the world, not because of foreseen faith, and the chain is unbroken: all those called are justified and glorified (Westminster Confession 3; Canons of Dort I). Barth rethought this: Jesus Christ is both the elect and the rejected one, and all are elected in him.

Election is in Christ, and the cause of the salvation of the elect; it is not the cause of the damnation of the lost, who perish by their own fault. The Formula of Concord warns against looking into God's hidden will (Solid Declaration XI).

God predestines no one to hell. Predestination to glory is real and part of providence (Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I.23), but no one can claim to know that he is predestined (Trent, session 6, chapter 12). Dominicans (Thomists) and Jesuits (Molinists) disagreed for centuries on how God's choice and human freedom fit.

Many Orthodox theologians read 8:29 as God's foreknowledge of the free response of each person. They emphasize synergy: grace and the human will work together. Predestination is God's will that all be saved, not a decree that shuts anyone out.

God foreknew who would believe and decided beforehand that they would be conformed to Christ; election is conditional on faith, and grace can be resisted (Wesley, "Predestination Calmly Considered"; Arminius, Analysis of Romans 9).

Article 17 teaches that predestination to life is God's everlasting purpose, "whereby (before the foundations of the world were laid) he hath constantly decreed by his counsel secret to us, to deliver from curse and damnation those whom he hath chosen in Christ out of mankind."

Baptists are divided. Particular Baptists hold Reformed election (1689 Confession, chapter 3); General Baptists hold election in view of faith. The Baptist Faith and Message (2000, article 5) calls election "the gracious purpose of God" that is "consistent with the free agency of man."

traditions.q: Can a believer lose salvation, if nothing can separate us from the love of God (8:38-39)?
views: Perseverance of the saints: those whom God has effectually called cannot totally or finally fall away, but will certainly persevere to the end (Westminster Confession 17; Canons of Dort V).
Southern Baptists teach that all true believers endure to the end (Baptist Faith and Message, 2000, article 5). General Baptists teach that a person can turn from faith and be lost.

Wesley taught that a believer can fall from grace. The promise of 8:38-39 is that no outside power can separate us, but a person can turn from God by his own unbelief (Wesley, "Serious Thoughts on the Perseverance of the Saints"; Methodist Articles of Religion, on sin after justification).

Believers can fall away through unbelief, yet the elect are kept by God, and comfort lies in the promise, not in watching oneself. The Augsburg Confession (XII) rejects those who deny that the justified can lose the Holy Spirit.

A person in grace can lose it by mortal sin. No one can be certain of final perseverance without a special revelation, but believers may hope in God's help (Council of Trent, session 6, chapter 13 and canon 16; Catechism 162, 1821).
Salvation is a path on which a person may fall away by free will. God's love is never withdrawn, but one may turn from it.
"After we have received the Holy Ghost, we may depart from grace given, and fall into sin, and by the grace of God we may arise again, and amend our lives" (Thirty-Nine Articles, Article 16).
Many Pentecostal churches (such as the Assemblies of God) teach that a believer can turn away from Christ and lose salvation; some Pentecostal bodies of Baptist background teach eternal security.
